# Adult mortality by household wealth: all estimates

All published estimates in
[`data/adult_mortality_gradients.csv`](../../data/adult_mortality_gradients.csv),
one row per country, census or survey, sex and age band. Methods are described
in [adult mortality from household-death records](../methods/adult-mortality.md);
countries without an estimate use the [general gradient](../methods/general-gradient.md).

In censuses, households are ranked by an asset index, the first principal
component of indicators for household assets and toilet type; the assets used
differ by census and are recorded in the census scripts
(`scripts/build_adult_mortality.py`, and `_brazil.py` and `_colombia.py` for the
two censuses taken from the statistical office's own microdata). Colombia 2018
is a full count; its deaths are those of calendar year 2017, and its index has
the fewest items (electricity, internet and toilet type). In surveys (India's
NFHS, through the DHS Program, and Bangladesh's Maternal Mortality and Health
Care Survey, BMMS), households are ranked by the survey's own wealth index, and
deaths are those of the two years before the interview
(`scripts/build_adult_mortality_survey.py`). `45q15` is the probability
of dying between ages 15 and 60; `mx` is the age-specific death rate for the
band shown. The low/high ratio is the rate in the lowest wealth group divided
by the rate in the highest. The standard error measures sampling variability
only: for surveys it is a cluster bootstrap (sampling clusters resampled within
strata); for censuses it treats each wealth group's death count as Poisson. It
leaves out errors in the wealth ranking and in the recording of deaths, which
are usually larger; the scatter of countries around the
[general gradient](../methods/general-gradient.md) is several times larger. "Linked" is the share of the census's death
records matched to household assets; survey death records are part of the
household interview and are all linked.

Where the census records the number of deaths per household (`MORTNUM`), the
weighted death records are compared with that number within each wealth group;
`scripts/build_adult_mortality.py` prints the comparison for every sample.
Uniform under-recording does not affect a gradient; under-recording that varies
with wealth does. The check could not be made for South Africa 2001 or Côte
d'Ivoire 1998, which do not record `MORTNUM`. In Colombia 2018 the death records
and the household's count of deaths come from the same questionnaire and agree
exactly, so the check is satisfied by construction and cannot detect lost
records. Samples that fail these checks are not published; they are listed
with the reasons on the
[adult-mortality page](../methods/adult-mortality.md#samples-not-published).

Age-band rates (`mx`) and 45q15 are published only where they rest on at least
900 death records; `Deaths` gives the number of records behind each estimate.
Rates are per 1,000.
